title: Grieved by your suffering
hookLine: a messenger from among you, grieved by your suffering, kind and merciful (9:128)
last: THE EARTH FELT NARROW, THEN WIDE.

cards: A month ago, with 'Isa's answer at the end of al-Ma'idah, you heard in passing that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once wept over that verse. Here is the whole report, from Muslim's collection.
He was reciting verses where Ibrahim speaks to God about his people, and then 'Isa does the same. He raised his hands and said: my community, my community. And he wept.
God sent Jibril to ask him why he was weeping, though God already knew. And the answer came back: We will please you concerning your community, and We will not grieve you.
Near the very end of at-Tawbah, a verse describes the man who wept.

teach.b: Verse one hundred twenty-eight, in paraphrase: there has come to you a messenger from among yourselves.
Whatever burdens you weighs heavy on him. He is deeply concerned for you, and to the believers he is kind and merciful. Take it a phrase at a time.
From among yourselves: not a stranger, not an angel, a man who grew up in their streets. Then: 'azizun 'alayhi ma 'anittum. What you suffer is hard on him.
Then: harisun 'alaykum, eager for you, anxious that things go well for you. A hadith in Bukhari gives a picture of that anxiety.

teach.h: HOLDING YOU BACK FROM THE FIRE.
teach.b: The Prophet said: my likeness and yours is like a man who lit a fire, and moths and insects keep flying into it, and I'm holding you by your belts, pulling you back from the flames.
Then two words: ra'uf, rahim, kind and merciful. Commentators point out that ar-Ra'uf and ar-Rahim are both names of God.
In this one verse, the Qur'an gives them to the Prophet as qualities, without making him more than a man. Notice the direction, too. The verse doesn't tell anyone to feel for the Prophet.
It says he already feels for you.
This is the second-to-last verse of a surah full of armies, excuses and hard warnings, and it ends with a portrait of tenderness.
Whatever you're carrying today, the portrait says, someone carried the worry of it long before you arrived.

how: Many Muslims recite the last two verses of at-Tawbah as part of their daily remembrance, and send blessings on the Prophet, sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam, each time his name is mentioned.

o: strict and just, a judge who weighs every deed
kind and merciful, the Qur'an's words for the Prophet
proud and mighty, a ruler over the believers

games.q: inside the portrait — tap the pairs.
p: kind and merciful; also names of God

s: 9:128 tells believers to feel sorry for the Prophet
it runs the other way: your suffering weighs on him.
ra'uf and rahim are also names of God
the verse gives the Prophet these qualities without making him more than a man.
the Prophet once wept, saying 'my community, my community'
in Muslim's collection; God sent word: We will please you concerning your community.

games.q: the Prophet recites verses where earlier prophets speak to God about their people. what does he do next, in Muslim's hadith?
o: he raises his hands, says 'my community,' and weeps.
he moves on to the next verse.
he asks the companions to pray for him.
games.why: he wept for his community, and God sent Jibril with the message: We will please you concerning your community.

practice: Think of one person who is struggling right now, and don't solve it; just let their trouble be hard on you for a few breaths, the way the verse describes.
If you pray, you can send peace and blessings on the Prophet, as many Muslims do whenever his name is said, or ask for the person by name.

wordCard.voice: Ra'uf rahim, kind and merciful. The Qur'an's portrait of the Prophet in 9:128: your hardship is hard on him, he is eager for your good.

orig.note: Arabic: kind and merciful, the last words of 9:128; both are also among the names of God.

carryVoice: Your line: he felt it with you. Feeling it comes before fixing it. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6483 (the man who lit a fire, and the moths)
